notes:
I've written these notes from the pages I read. A few gaps up front:

- **Missing sources.** I found nothing on Orthodox readings (oca.org) or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- **Pentecostal and Anglican views.** The only source from your Pentecostal/charismatic list is Enduring Word (David Guzik). His notes are general evangelical teaching rather than a distinctly Pentecostal view, and no Anglican source on these verses said where it stood as a tradition.
- **Enduring Word coverage.** My copy of Guzik's full text stops at v. 20. For vv. 21–31 I relied on the page's summary, which the site says is AI-generated.

**v. 1–2**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says Romans 2 showed that having the law and circumcision won't save a Jewish person, so Paul now asks what the advantage of being God's chosen nation is. His answer is that God entrusted them with His written revelation before Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Matthew Henry calls the Jews "the Christians' library-keepers." The Jews had the means of salvation, but they had not the monopoly of salvation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_003.cfm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** he takes "oracles" to mean the scriptures, in which are so great and precious promises. He adds that more privileges are listed in Romans 9:4–5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-3.html
- **Modern scholarship:** the NET note says readers have taken "oracles" three ways. BDAG says God's promises to the Jews. Some say only the national promises of a coming Messiah. The most common view is the whole Old Testament. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3

**v. 3–4**
- Guzik says the Jewish people's general rejection of the gospel did not make God's faithfulness to them pointless. In the end God will be shown right in everything He does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Precept Austin notes that the Psalm 51 quotation shows God was right to punish David's sin. So God's faithfulness covers both blessing and curse, and it does not rule out judging Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_31
- Wesley reads the verse as a question: will God not still keep His promises to those who do believe? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-3.html

**v. 5–6**
- Guzik describes the objection as "my sin brings God more glory, so how can He judge me?" Paul's answer: if that were true, God could judge no one. One way God gets glory from human sin is by judging it rightly. "I speak as a man" means only a fallen man would dare question God's justice; it does not mean Paul was speaking without inspiration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Matthew Henry: sin is no less wicked because God brings glory out of it. Sin only shows off God's righteousness by accident. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_003.cfm

**v. 7–8**
- Barnes says God's truth is shown when He carries out His warnings as well as His promises. Every lost sinner will be, therefore, an eternal monument of the truth of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/romans-3.html
- Guzik: "let us do evil that good may come" twisted Paul's teaching on justification. He adds that you can see how the charge arose, given how freely Paul preached grace. If a preacher today is accused of preaching grace too freely, he is in good company with Paul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Wesley says Paul refuses to answer directly and cuts the objector short with a rebuke. In doing so, the apostle absolutely denies the lawfulness of doing evil, any evil, that good may come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: "we" means "we Jews." "Under sin" pictures slavery to sin, and he quotes Morris on sin as a tyrant that sinners cannot escape. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Wesley says "under sin" means under the guilt and power of it: the Jews, by transgressing the written law; the gentiles, by transgressing the law of nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm

**v. 10–12**
- **Sources quoted:** the NET notes say vv. 10–12 quote Psalm 14:1–3. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3
- **Guzik:** there has never been a truly righteous man apart from Christ. When people start the search themselves, they don't find the God of the Bible; they find an idol they made. "Unprofitable" carries the idea of rotten fruit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- **Wesley's nuance:** he says David and Isaiah described the people of their own day. They showed what manner of men God sees, when he "looks down from heaven;" not what he makes them by his grace. He takes "unprofitable" to mean helpless and powerless. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/ and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- Barnes: the Psalm describes the "children of men" at large, not only Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/romans-3.html

**v. 13–17**
- Guzik: Paul names throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet and eyes, showing that the fall reaches every part of a person. He quotes Wiersbe calling it "an X-ray study" of the lost sinner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Wesley traces evil speech moving from the heart through the throat, tongue and lips until it fills the whole mouth. He takes "cursing" as aimed at God and "bitterness" as aimed at one's neighbour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Sources quoted:** Psalms 5:9, 140:3 and 10:7, and Isaiah 59:7–8 for vv. 15–17. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3

**v. 18**
- Guzik says this verse sums up the whole list: every sin comes from a lack of proper reverence for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Wesley: if there is no fear of God before their eyes, there is even less love of God in their hearts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-3.html

**v. 19**
- Guzik: many Jews of Paul's day applied Old Testament descriptions of evil only to Gentiles. Paul shows they were addressed to those under the law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Wesley: the verses were quoted not to make men criminal, but to prove them so. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-3.html

**v. 20 (a point where views differ: what are "works of the law"?)**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says a broken law can only condemn. Even keeping it perfectly from now on could not make up for past disobedience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Paul means chiefly the moral part of the law, the part that is not abolished (v. 31). The law brings knowledge of sin but no rescue from its guilt or power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Desiring God (Baptist; the author isn't named in what I saw):** the article takes "works of the law" to mean all efforts at law-keeping, and it calls the New Perspective on Paul "fading away." https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/faith-alone
- **Modern scholarship:** the NET note sets out the debate. Dunn takes "works of the law" to mean the parts of the law that marked Jews off from other nations, such as circumcision and food laws. Cranfield rejects this narrow reading, partly because "through the law comes the knowledge of sin" is hard to explain on it. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3
- **Catholic:** catholic.com says the "works of the Law" are works required by the Law of Moses. https://www.catholic.com/audio/tjap/faith-alone-what-everybody-gets-wrong

**v. 21**
- Guzik's page summary calls "But now" the great turning point of the chapter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- Wesley: "righteousness of God" means the way of becoming righteous that God has appointed, and "the Law and the Prophets" means all the Old Testament promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** the NET note says most recent interpreters take "But now" as a time marker, the start of a new phase in salvation history. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3

**v. 22 (debated: "faith in Christ" or "faithfulness of Christ"?)**
- **Traditional reading:** Calvin says the phrase means not the faith which is his, but the faith of which he is the object. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/3-22.html
- **Wesley:** "to all" means the Jews and "upon all" means the Gentiles. There is no difference between them in either their need of justification or the way they receive it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** NET translates "faithfulness of Jesus Christ" and notes that more and more scholars hold this view (Hays, Hooker). Its main argument is grammatical: when "faith" is followed by a person in this form, it almost always means that person's own faith. NET also says most commentaries still take the traditional view. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3
- **Bible.org:** this exposition also prefers "Christ's faithfulness," meaning His obedience to the Father in life and death. https://bible.org/seriespage/9-study-and-exposition-romans-321-31
- **Bible Odyssey:** the "faithfulness" reading removes the repetition in "faith in Christ … for all who believe." Paul may be using the ambiguity on purpose. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/faith-of-christ/
- **The Gospel Coalition:** a review describes the scholarly debate. Campbell argues for "faithfulness of Christ," while Matlock argues that Christ is the object of faith. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/the-faith-of-jesus-christ-exegetical-biblical-and-theological-studies-the-pistis-christou-debate/
- **Coffman (in the StudyLight collection):** he rejects changing the translation, saying it serves to prop up a "faith only" view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/3-22.html

**v. 23**
- **Ellicott:** the Greek is strictly "all sinned," looking back at a past act whose effect carries into the present. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/3-23.htm
- **Poole (Reformed):** both Jew and Gentile have the guilt of Adam's transgression imputed to them, along with inherited corruption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/3-23.htm
- **Wesley:** all have sinned "in Adam, and in their own persons." "The glory of God" is the supreme purpose of human life: His image on earth and enjoying Him in heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- Other commentators on the same page read "glory" differently. Vincent takes it as God's approval. The Geneva notes take it as everlasting life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/3-23.htm

**v. 24**
- **Guzik:** justification answers our guilt, redemption answers our slavery, and propitiation answers our offence against God. He quotes Calvin that the doubled "freely … by grace" leaves nothing to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- **Wesley:** justified means "pardoned and accepted," and redemption is the price Christ paid. On the doubled wording he writes that It is not possible to find words that should more absolutely exclude all consideration of our own works and obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm

**v. 25 (debated: propitiation, expiation, or mercy seat?)**
- **Reformed (The Gospel Coalition):** the word means propitiation. God Himself put Jesus forward as a sacrifice that turned away His own just anger at sin. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/propitiation/
- **Reformed (Monergism):** this source also prefers "propitiatory sacrifice" over "mercy seat." https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/questions/propitiation.pdf
- **Precept Austin:** the sacrifice bears God's wrath and turns it into favour. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_325-26
- **Wesley (Methodist):** propitiation means "to appease an offended God." If God was never offended, Christ died in vain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Ellicott:** he leans toward "sacrifice" rather than "mercy seat," because Christ was displayed publicly and the verse mentions His blood. He translates it as a propitiatory or expiatory sacrifice. He also admits we can't fully say in what sense our punishment fell on Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/3-25.htm
- **Meyer:** Chrysostom read it as "expiatory sacrifice," and faith is what makes the sacrifice effective for the person who believes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/3-25.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** NET translates "mercy seat." Its note says that reading clashes with "in his blood" if both describe Jesus, so it attaches "in his blood" to the verb ("at his death"). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3
- **"Sins committed beforehand":** Benson says God's long patience with past sins could have made His justice look doubtful. The cross proves His justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/3-25.htm

**v. 26**
- Guzik's summary: God is both just, because the penalty was paid, and the justifier of those who trust in Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
- **Wesley:** God shows His justice on His own Son, so all the attributes harmonize. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Barnes (a different view of substitution):** Christ took the sinner's place, but not by suffering the exact penalty. His sufferings achieved the same ends. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/romans-3.html
- **NET:** translates "the one who lives because of Jesus' faithfulness," with "has faith in Jesus" as the alternative. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=rom&chapter=3

**v. 27**
- **Wesley:** this is the Jew's boasting over the Gentile. The "law of faith" is God's arrangement that makes faith, not works, the condition of acceptance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Sproul (Reformed, Ligonier):** no merit from our works contributes to the ground of our justification. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/boasting-excluded

**v. 28 (the sharpest divide: "faith alone")**
- **Reformed:** The Gospel Coalition says Luther was right to translate it "by faith alone." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/faith-and-works/
- **Reformed (Sproul):** he grants that "alone" is not in the Greek. But being justified apart from works of the law is the same as being justified by faith alone. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/boasting-excluded
- **Lutheran (1517):** this is called the most Lutheran verse in Scripture. If justification is apart from works, it is by faith alone, *sola fide*. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-romans-319-28-reformation-sunday-series-a-2023
- **Baptist (Desiring God):** affirms Luther's rendering. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/faith-alone
- **Methodist (Wesley):** we are justified by faith, but not as it is a work, but as it receives Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Catholic:** catholic.com agrees justification comes by faith, but says it does not come through faith alone. Luther added "alone," which is not in the Greek. The only place Scripture uses "faith alone" is James 2:24, which rejects it. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/arent-we-saved-by-faith-alone
- A second catholic.com piece makes the same point: "apart from works of the law" cannot be turned into "alone." https://www.catholic.com/audio/tjap/faith-alone-what-everybody-gets-wrong

**v. 29–30**
- **Wesley:** God is the God of Gentiles too, as nature and Scripture show, and He shows mercy to both groups by the same means. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Catholic:** catholic.com says Paul's follow-up question, "Is God the God of Jews only?", shows he is talking about the Law of Moses. https://www.catholic.com/audio/tjap/faith-alone-what-everybody-gets-wrong
- **Guzik's summary:** both circumcised and uncircumcised are justified by faith alone, because one God rules over all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/

**v. 31**
- **Wesley:** faith upholds the law's authority, purity and purpose. It does this by defending what the law witnesses to, by pointing to Christ as its goal, and by showing how it can be fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/3.htm
- **Barnes:** Christ's suffering to show the evil of breaking the law is a strong motive for obeying it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/romans-3.html
- **Guzik's summary:** the gospel fulfils what the law itself predicted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-3/
